stem: Which of these is a chemical change?
options: Ice cubes melting in a glass of water.
An iron gate rusting after months of rain.
Sugar dissolving in a cup of hot tea.
A glass bottle breaking into pieces.
working: A chemical change forms one or more new substances.
Rust is a new substance, formed when iron reacts with oxygen from the air in the presence of water, so rusting is a chemical change.
Melting, dissolving and breaking change only the state, the mixing or the shape. No new substance is formed, so they are physical changes.
Watch out: Dissolving is a physical change. The sugar is still sugar, and you can get it back by evaporating the water.

distractors.1: Melting is a change of state. The water is still water and can freeze again: no new substance is formed.
distractors.3: Dissolving is a physical change. The sugar is still there, and evaporating the water gets it back.
distractors.4: Breaking changes only the shape and size of the pieces. They are still glass.

hints: Ask of each change: is a new substance made, or is it the same substance in a new state, shape or mixture?
Which change leaves behind a substance with different properties from the one you started with?

stem: Wei Ming adds small pieces of zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid in a test tube. Bubbles of gas are given off. Which test identifies this gas?
options: Bubble the gas through limewater: the limewater turns chalky (a white precipitate forms).
Put a glowing splint into the test tube: the splint relights.
Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas: the paper turns red.
Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the test tube: the splint goes out with a 'pop' sound.
working: An acid reacts with a metal to give a salt and hydrogen: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.
The test for hydrogen: a lighted splint held at the mouth of the test tube goes out with a 'pop' sound.
Watch out: A glowing splint that relights is the test for OXYGEN. Hydrogen needs a LIGHTED splint and gives a pop.

distractors.1: Limewater tests for carbon dioxide, which an acid gives off with a carbonate, not with a metal.
distractors.2: A glowing splint relighting is the test for oxygen. An acid and a metal do not give off oxygen.
distractors.3: Litmus shows whether a gas is acidic, not which gas it is. Hydrogen is neutral, so this is not its test.

hints: First name the gas: what does an acid make when it reacts with a metal?
Each common gas has its own splint or limewater test. Which test goes with this gas?

stem: Nurul adds dilute hydrochloric acid to some marble chips (calcium carbonate). The mixture fizzes. Which general word equation describes this reaction?
options: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
acid + carbonate → salt + hydrogen
acid + carbonate → salt + water
acid + carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide
working: Marble chips are a carbonate, so this is an acid reacting with a carbonate.
acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. The fizzing is the carbon dioxide gas being given off.
Compare the other two: acid + alkali → salt + water; acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.
Watch out: Learn the three acid equations side by side. Only the carbonate gives carbon dioxide; only the metal gives hydrogen.

distractors.2: Hydrogen comes from an acid reacting with a METAL, not with a carbonate.
distractors.3: Salt + water only is what an acid and an ALKALI give (neutralisation). A carbonate also gives off carbon dioxide, which causes the fizzing.
distractors.4: A carbonate breaks down into a metal oxide and carbon dioxide when it is HEATED strongly (thermal decomposition). No acid is involved in that.

hints: The fizzing tells you a gas is made. Which gas comes from a carbonate?
Recall the three acid reactions: with an alkali, with a metal and with a carbonate. Which products go with the carbonate?

stem: Hui Min puts an open flask of dilute acid and a small dish of marble chips together on an electronic balance. The balance reads 152.40 g. She tips the chips into the acid, and the mixture fizzes for a few minutes. What happens to the balance reading, and why?
options: It increases, because new substances are formed in the flask.
It stays at 152.40 g, because mass is always conserved in a chemical reaction.
It decreases, because carbon dioxide gas escapes from the open flask into the air.
It decreases, because some atoms are destroyed as the chips react.
working: Mass is conserved in every chemical reaction: the atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.
But the flask is open. The carbon dioxide made in the reaction escapes into the air, so its mass is no longer on the balance.
The reading therefore falls. In a sealed flask the gas could not escape, and the reading would stay at 152.40 g.
Watch out: 'Mass is conserved' counts ALL the products, gases included. Ask whether everything stays on the balance.

distractors.1: New substances form, but the atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass cannot go up. Here a gas also leaves the flask.
distractors.2: True only if nothing can escape, as in a sealed flask. Here the flask is open and the gas escapes.
distractors.4: Atoms are never destroyed in a chemical reaction. The mass missing from the balance is in the gas that escaped.

hints: What do you see when the chips meet the acid? Where does that gas go?
Mass is conserved for everything the reaction makes. Is everything still on the balance at the end?

stem:
An indicator can be made by soaking blue pea flowers in hot water. The table shows the colour of this extract in solutions of known pH.

| pH | Colour of the extract |
| --- | --- |
| 2 | pink |
| 4 | purple |
| 7 | blue |
| 10 | green |
| 13 | yellow |

In a class demonstration, the teacher adds the extract to three liquids. Lime juice turns it pink, soapy water turns it green and a dilute oven cleaner turns it yellow. Which statement is correct?
options: The soapy water is neutral, because green is in the middle of the colour range.
The lime juice is alkaline, because pink is at one end of the colour range.
The oven cleaner is the most strongly alkaline of the three liquids.
Red litmus paper would show which of the two alkaline liquids is more strongly alkaline.
working: Match each colour to the table: pink is about pH 2, green about pH 10 and yellow about pH 13.
Lime juice (about pH 2) is strongly acidic. Soapy water (about pH 10) is alkaline. The oven cleaner (about pH 13) is the most strongly alkaline.
Litmus only shows whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. An indicator with many colours, like this extract or Universal Indicator, also shows how acidic or alkaline it is.
Watch out: Neutral is pH 7, which is blue for this extract, not green.

distractors.1: Neutral is pH 7, which turns this extract blue. Green matches about pH 10, so the soapy water is alkaline.
distractors.2: Pink matches about pH 2. A pH below 7 means acidic, so lime juice is acidic.
distractors.4: Red litmus turns blue in ANY alkali. It cannot tell a weakly alkaline solution from a strongly alkaline one.

hints: Use the table: write down the pH that matches each colour seen.
The further the pH is above 7, the more strongly alkaline the solution.

stem:
Ahmad heats some green copper(II) carbonate powder in a test tube. The powder turns black, and a gas is given off that turns limewater chalky.

Name this type of chemical change, write a word equation for the reaction, and explain how the observations show that it is a chemical change.
answer: Thermal decomposition: one substance is broken down by heat into two or more simpler substances. Word equation: copper(II) carbonate → copper(II) oxide + carbon dioxide. It is a chemical change because new substances are formed: a black solid (copper(II) oxide) that is different from the green powder, and a gas that turns limewater chalky (carbon dioxide).
working: Heat breaks one substance down into simpler ones, so this is thermal decomposition. A metal carbonate breaks down into the metal oxide and carbon dioxide: copper(II) carbonate → copper(II) oxide + carbon dioxide.
A chemical change forms new substances. The evidence: a black solid with different properties from the green powder, and a gas that turns limewater chalky, which is carbon dioxide.
Common error: Calling it combustion. Combustion is burning in oxygen; here the powder is broken down by heat alone.
hints: Is anything burning here, or is one substance being broken down by heat?
The limewater tells you the gas. What is left of a metal carbonate when that gas is driven off by heat?
marking: 1 mark: thermal decomposition. 'Decomposition' alone or 'combustion' scores 0: nothing burns and no oxygen is used.
1 mark: copper(II) carbonate → copper(II) oxide + carbon dioxide (accept copper carbonate and copper oxide).
1 mark: new substances are formed, shown by the black solid and by the gas turning limewater chalky (carbon dioxide).

stem:
Kumar sets up three test tubes, each with an identical clean iron nail, and leaves them for one week.

| Tube | Conditions | Nail after one week |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | tap water, open to the air | rusty |
| B | water that was boiled to remove dissolved air, with a layer of oil on top | not rusty |
| C | dry air (a drying agent removes water vapour), stoppered | not rusty |

Explain why the layer of oil is added in tube B, and use the results to state what iron needs in order to rust.
answer: The oil stops air from dissolving back into the boiled water, so the nail in B has water but no air (oxygen). Iron needs both air (oxygen) and water to rust: A had both and rusted; B had water but no air and did not rust; C had air but no water and did not rust.
working: Rusting is an oxidation: iron reacts with oxygen from the air in the presence of water.
Boiling removes the dissolved air, and the oil layer stops air dissolving back in, so tube B tests 'water without air'.
Tube C tests 'air without water'. Tube A has both and is the only rusty nail, so both are needed.
Common error: Writing 'iron needs water' or 'iron needs air' alone. The data show it needs both, and the answer must refer to the tubes.
hints: Boiling took the air out of the water in tube B. What could get back in if there were no oil?
Make a list: which tubes have air, and which have water? Compare it with which nails rusted.
keywords: oil keeps air out of the water
marking: 1 mark: the oil stops air (oxygen) from dissolving into the water.
1 mark: iron needs both air (oxygen) and water to rust.
1 mark: supported by the tubes, e.g. B (no air) and C (no water) did not rust, while A (air and water) did.
